title: The Fruits of Covetousness
english: Accompanying him to the tombs, walking healthily.

If he mounts the horse in a hurry, he is filled with pride; if he obtains more abundant food, he grumbles; if he wakes the servants early for their services, he is vexed by their waking and by the strength of the old man. But if he is given something of his treasures or if a servant is released from service, then and only then does he become a source of idle talk and wandering, exceeding the bounds of life and the things of others, a sword of the stranger, and he is provoked by hearing all blasphemy, asking why he did not die quickly.

Yours is this, O filthy greed, the fruit; from you the child becomes an enemy to the one who begot him, taking the stings. You fill the earth with robbers and murderers, submerge the sea, the cities with uproar, the courts with false witnesses, informers, traitors, accomplices, and judges who rule there wherever you drag them down.

Greed, the mother of inequality, pitiless, misanthropic, most wretched. Because of this, the life of man is full of irregularity; some, from the abundance of their possessions, sail upon the surplus as if it were an insatiable food, while others are pressed by hunger and want.

Some lie down under golden roofs and inhabit houses like small cities, adorned with baths, varied houses, and porticoes serving for a very long time and with every kind of luxury; others do not seem to have a roof, but when they cannot live in the open air, they flee to the furnaces of the baths or encounter bad innkeepers, and like pigs they root in the dung, devising for themselves the necessary warmth.

And the human being, the animal that is alike, has such a difference in diet compared to the kind that is alike; no one else has this disorder and this irregularity being introduced by greed. One is unseemly with his meals being meager, and another, to have his walls clothed in countless purple slabs, dresses them. The poor man lacks bread upon a wooden table, and the one enjoying luxury is entertained by the luster of the material, having spread a silver table wide. And how much more just was it for one to be satisfied with eating by another luxury, while the value of the table is the luxury of the destitute?

Another, old and unable to walk or limping due to some infirmity, does not possess a donkey, a necessary vehicle for his need; and another, because of a multitude of herds, does not know his horses. One is in want of oil to light a lamp; and another is rich with single lamps. One is thrown upon the ground, and the one who is wretchedly rich is surrounded by the world of the bed, having a silver sphere and chains instead of sheets.

These are the results of insatiable greed. For if it had not introduced inequality into life, these extremes and commonnesses would not have been, nor would the various misfortunes make our life unpleasantly tearful.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Root of Conflict and Divine Providence
english: From this, men have destroyed natural friendship toward one another; they sharpen iron, form battle lines, and like wild beasts, they seize one another with great ferocity.

How could anyone even explain what follows this? Walls are besieged by engines, cities are plundered, women are led away, and children are enslaved; the earth is cut and plowed, and trees are fought over as if they were humans who had done wrong; and the slaughter of those in their prime is great, and the streams of blood flow from the wretched bodies; and the wealth of the defeated is the prize of the victors.

Upon these things are the wails of bereavement, the tears of orphans, and the lamenting of father and child together, and of liberty. The former master of great wealth now begs for a morsel of bread, stretching out his right hand; and he who once had many slaves, weaving fabrics and filling houses with clothing, now wears a rag and serves, carrying water out of necessity and unhitching the horse's pole and performing shameful services; and ten thousand other evils, which it is impossible to take in at once.

The beginning, cause, and root of all these things is the desire for more, the unjust love of the property of others. If anyone had cut off this passion of men, he would not have prevented peace from being lived deeply, nor wars and disturbances from fleeing from men, but all would have returned to natural affection and friendship.

For this reason also our Lord carefully allows this disease to pass by, sometimes forbidding: 'You cannot serve God and mammon' (Matt 6:24); sometimes rejecting that wretched rich man, who was about to die soon and was setting before himself the long-lasting enjoyment of luxury as a model; and elsewhere teaching that the perfect man is he who, having given away all that he has to those in need, will go his own way toward virtuous philosophy, the mother and companion of all things.

But I think I hear, even while being silent, such things being said to the teachers by those accustomed to them: 'And how shall we manage life if the possession of money is neglected? How shall we suffice for our needs? How shall a debt be settled? And how shall a loan be given to the one seeking, if we are all destitute because of your advice?' Unbelieving is the word, senseless is the voice, not knowing that we have God as Master, the steward of life, who provides for the living being from himself the useful things and the necessary supplies of food and the need of clothing.

For the providence of God regarding the things of His own is all-encompassing; and He has never withheld calamity from one who prospers in faith. And bringing forward one of the divine sayings as a sufficient testimony for what is at hand, I think, I shall provide a witness. In the history of the Kingdoms...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Widow and Elisha
english: A certain woman is written about, a widow, being greatly weighed down by the misfortune of loneliness. A money-loving and misanthropic creditor was besieging her, taking away her sons, whom the mother had as her only ones instead of all. And when the matter stood for her in helplessness and no one having gold showed mercy, she came to the one possessing philanthropy and faith.

And this Elisha was the prophet, a man of the earthly substances being generous and abounding in the incorporeal possession; a philosopher from plowmen, unhoused, without support, living alone; having inherited recently, and having received the inheritance a widow's jar and an invisible blessing descending from the fiery chariot. He did not by any means send the entreaty unworked, nor did he reject the help because the sought-after thing was not present, nor did he say any base or faithless words, like one of the many: 'And from where to me is silver, so as to dissolve the debt?'

Just as an excellent physician and pharmacist, when not present, found the cure for the disease from extraordinary thoughts, so he says, 'What to you, O woman, upon the house? Remember if there is even a little inside.' For no one is so poor as to be suddenly the master of nothing. And as he said, that it is a jar and a little remnant of oil in it, 'Prepare for me,' he said, 'a multitude of vessels.' And she hurried, and he through it filled them, and to the creditor the debt was dissolved; and the woman departed from helplessness finding a way.

For the very little oil, which was to be with her, she said to the prophet, filled from the extraordinary and all the prepared amphorae; and then the flow stood, when there was no longer a vessel to receive; and to the need the grace was measured. Truly that was oil, which the plant did not bear, but the mercies of God flourished.

Acquire this knowledge, if you are able, kings, rulers, the wealthy, from the sun setting until it rises twice. You, the wise of the worldly wisdom, acquire the gift of the prophet from the plowmen, which was inexhaustible to the one receiving it. For the possessions of your zeal have myriad dangers lying in wait: robbers breaking through walls, tyrants snatching, and informers attacking, the sea sinking, and the earth being cracked by chasms.

Let there therefore be hope and a storehouse for men, the right hand of God, which led the people of Egypt out and in a desert land provided the abundance of good things; which led the Ambakum to Daniel, and saved Ishmael having been cast off from the mother's embrace, and sufficed to each generation, and lastly multiplied five barley loaves as if infinite agriculture, so that one loaf might fill the stomach of a thousand starving men and be enough for the basket of the remnants. To our God be the glory unto the ages of ages. Amen.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
